articles.title: A who's who of tech showed up for Trump's dinner with Xi — with one glaring exception
articles.summary: Donald Trump's dinner with China's leader, Xi Jinping, is shaping up to be a gathering of tech's biggest names.
articles.body:
Donald Trump is hosting China's leader to discuss tariffs, critical minerals, and AI safety.

The attendees included AMD CEO Lisa Su, OpenAI's Sam Altman, and Elon Musk.

Here are the biggest names in tech who showed up for dinner at the White House.

Donald Trump's dinner with China's leader, Xi Jinping, on Thursday was a glitzy gathering of the biggest names in tech.

AMD CEO Lisa Su said during a fireside chat at the New York Stock Exchange that she will be attending Thursday's White House event, joining executives expected to include Nvidia's Jensen Huang, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Alphabet's Sundar Pichai, Tesla's Elon Musk, and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos.

Dario Amodei, the Anthropic CEO who also led the call for more cautious AI development, was notably absent from the dinner.

Plenty is riding on the talks. Washington and Beijing are negotiating amid a trade truce, with tariffs, critical minerals, and semiconductors among the issues at stake. The US has also proposed a channel for the two countries to notify each other about significant AI safety incidents, which remains under discussion.

"I think technology is one of those areas where we rely on the global ecosystem to come together," Su told Fox Business's Liz Claman in a fireside chat on Wednesday, adding she was "honored" to join the White House dinner.

"So, yes, I think we're anxiously looking at what will come out of it," Su said. "And the truth is, we want to ensure that there's good stability across the global ecosystem as it relates to technology."

In clockwise order, Trump's table consisted of himself, first lady Melania Trump, Musk, Su and her spouse, Daniel Lin, Jensen Huang and his spouse, Lori Huang, former Apple CEO Tim Cook , China's first lady Peng Liyuan, and China's leader Xi Jinping.

Vice President JD Vance and Usha Vance were seen seated at a different table to the right.

Altman spotted chatting with Mark Zuckerberg

The two tech CEOs have both recently weighed in on AI safety issues, as the topic is expected to be discussed with China's leader.

Altman has backed setting shared safety standards, including rules for when companies should slow or stop developing more powerful models, while Zuckerberg has said that AI labs have strong incentives to make their models safe and can decide for themselves when to slow down.

Jensen Huang spoke to other guests at the center table

Huang, dressed in more traditional business attire, was seated at the main table alongside Trump and Xi.

Nvidia has felt the tech rivalry between the US and China acutely over the past few years. After Washington imposed new export restrictions on Nvidia's H20 chips in April 2025, the company said it missed out on $2.5 billion in shipments that quarter and took a $4.5 billion charge tied to unsold inventory and purchase commitments.

As recently as August, Nvidia was still assuming no China data center chip revenue in its forecast.

SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk mingled with guests, including Anna Brockman

Musk and Brockman, the spouse of OpenAI cofounder and president Greg Brockman, are both heavyweight Trump donors.

Musk, in particular, holds major business interests in China due to Tesla's Gigafactory in Shanghai , which produces about half of the automaker's deliveries.

The world's richest man said earlier this month, during a podcast appearance, that the US and China should agree to peer review or test AI models from the leading firms in each other's countries.

Musk's SpaceX is also arguably the single most important company to the US space race against China, providing the bulk of American orbital launches and maintaining the world's largest satellite constellation.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai and Secretary of State Marco Rubio

The Google CEO was seen having an animated conversation with Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Google, one of the leading AI labs in the US, is investing heavily in AI capacity, with a total capex forecast of $195 billion to $205 billion this year. That's higher than most of the rest of Big Tech, except for Amazon , which estimates $220 billion in total capex in 2026.

Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sánchez Bezos

Amazon doesn't operate its marketplace in China, which has its own, far more domestically successful e-commerce platforms.

But the country has become a major supply and export hub for Amazon, to the point that the company built a global warehousing and distribution network this year in three major Chinese shipping ports to funnel goods to the US.

Bezos and Sánchez were just two representatives of America's corporate elite invited to Thursday's dinner — lead executives for BlackRock, JP Morgan, Goldman Sachs, LVMH, and Lockheed Martin were also among those present.

articles.title: ICE wasted millions in rapid push to expand detention capacity, watchdog finds
articles.summary: With an unprecedented budget, ICE spent billions in a rush to expand its detention network, wasting millions in the process, the Government Accountability Of...
articles.body:
In a single day in January, Immigration and Customs Enforcement spent more money than it had on any other day in either of President Trump's terms, federal spending records show.

The agency advanced billions to Chicago Title Insurance in escrow to acquire detention facilities, according to a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson. Over the next two months, ICE used $1.07 billion of the funds to purchase 11 warehouses it planned to convert to detention megacenters, seven of which the agency now plans to sell.

The rest of the money sat with the firm for months after ICE abandoned the warehouse plan. In July and August, ICE moved $2.2 billion from Chicago Title to purchase four detention facilities from CoreCivic, a private prison company it separately pays to continue operating them.

In its rush to expand detention capacity, ICE wasted millions of taxpayer dollars, the Government Accountability Office found in a report released Thursday. The agency failed to account for long-term costs in acquiring detention centers and lost $20 million in unrecoverable costs purchasing the warehouses it no longer plans to use, the review found. Even more could be lost if ICE sells the warehouses for less than what it paid for them, the GAO report said.

Barring any undisclosed purchases, $1.55 billion still sits with Chicago Title Insurance for acquiring detention centers as ICE continues its push to double the number of detention beds in service of the president's mass deportation agenda. Just this week, ICE awarded several companies contracts that could reach a combined $10 billion to expand and construct new facilities.

GAO concluded that "urgent planning" is necessary to reduce further waste. ICE said it would produce a strategic plan by Aug. 31, 2027, a date the watchdog said wasn't soon enough.

"We just saw a real lack of planning overall," said Heather MacLeod, director of Homeland Security and Justice at GAO. "The lack of planning has really led to stops and starts which have ultimately resulted in waste."

GAO's report did not estimate a total amount potentially lost to waste, but MacLeod said another review of ICE spending is currently underway.

Flush with cash after Congress funneled $75 billion to the agency — including $45 billion to expand detention capacity — through President Trump's " One Big Beautiful Bill Act ," ICE has nearly doubled its spending this year. The agency spent $19 billion from last October to July, the most recent month for which data is available, up from $11 billion the previous full fiscal year, a CBS News analysis of federal data found.

A DHS spokesperson wrote to CBS News that ICE is "working at turbo speed on cost-effective and innovative ways to deliver on the American people's mandate for mass deportations of criminal illegal aliens," and that the spending bill known as OBBBA has provided "historic funding" to help it carry out the mandate.

Appropriating funds outside of the typical process — and without the usual guardrails that come in appropriations bills — means ICE has more flexibility in how it can use the funding, said Kevin McNellis, a policy and budget analyst who previously worked in the Congressional Budget Office and Congressional Research Service. That also leads to a breakdown in oversight, he wrote in a report he authored for Co-Equal, a nonprofit focused on congressional authority.

"When DHS only had annual funding or relied on the annual appropriations for the majority of its funding, there were long standing systems and processes in place for DHS to inform Congress of its spending plan and for Congress to then oversee those spending plans," McNellis told CBS News. "The situation we've been in since OBBBA passed is we have an unprecedented amount of money, appropriated outside those long-standing processes, trying to be spent very quickly."

ICE paid an 11% to 13% premium on the 11 warehouses it purchased, according to CoStar, a real estate analytics firm. Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem directed ICE to purchase new detention sites within 30 days, contributing to the high prices, The Wall Street Journal reported .

The remaining warehouses ICE still hopes to convert face legal challenges, though ICE already signed contracts worth a combined $426 million to renovate two of them. No detainees are currently held in any of the warehouses.

After dropping the warehouse plan, ICE spent $1.47 billion purchasing two California detention facilities from CoreCivic in July. The next month, ICE bought another two CoreCivic facilities in Kansas and Minnesota for a combined $734 million. In its announcement of the August purchases, CoreCivic said the company is in talks with ICE to sell more facilities.

CoreCivic is using the profits from the sales to pay down its debts, according to company filings .

GAO found that ICE had only forecasted costs for these centers and to-be-converted warehouses for the next three years, failing to consider how it would pay for them once the funds Congress has allocated through 2029 run out.

The watchdog also found that through FEMA reimbursements, ICE paid the state of Florida almost triple its typical per-bed rate for two state-operated facilities, including the now-shuttered facility dubbed "Alligator Alcatraz." ICE skipped typical contract negotiation practices, creating a new grant program with the state of Florida as the only eligible recipient, according to the GAO report. FEMA paid Florida a total of $608.4 million for "Alligator Alcatraz," GAO said.

ICE is also paying more than it typically would per-bed to house noncitizen detainees at facilities operated by the Bureau of Prisons. BOP officials told GAO they've had to pay staff overtime and for temporary assignments to meet ICE's needs, resulting in a per-bed-rate double that of ICE's median rate.

Another abandoned initiative GAO cited was ICE's efforts to launch detention facilities at military bases, like the one at Camp East Montana in El Paso. A previous GAO review found ICE spent $7.1 million on detainee meals it did not need at the El Paso facility. ICE dropped its plan to launch similar facilities on military installations in Indiana and New Jersey, GAO reported.

ICE also spent $2.85 million on tents at Guantanamo Bay to house detainees that were never used. The facility, initially planned for 30,000 detainees, held only a handful. In May, CBS News reported that the Guantanamo Bay facility was holding just six detainees. The agency is still trying to house detainees on the naval base: this week it signed a contract with the same company it used to help procure the warehouses and acquire the CoreCivic facilities to construct a facility at Guantanamo Bay and at other sites.

DHS's Inspector General is conducting its own audit into ICE's acquisition of detention space to determine whether it made purchases in a "cost-effective manner." The internal watchdog is also probing ICE spending on air charter services and its reporting on how it is using Big Beautiful Bill funds.

"We think it's important that DHS and ICE do develop a plan going forward tied to their needs and what they're trying to get out of their expansion efforts," said MacLeod, the GAO director. "We're encouraged to see that they agreed with our recommendation and we're hoping they'll take steps to address it quickly."

articles.title: Ex-Dem insider blows lid off fundraising 'gimmicks' during 2024 election: 'Pyramid scheme'
articles.summary: Lindy Li reveals how Kamala Harris's billion-dollar war chest was funneled to media consultants, alleging fundraising gimmicks and lavish spending.
articles.body: Lindy Li, a former Democratic fundraiser who switched her party affiliation over unheeded warning signs of President Joe Biden’s decline in the 2024 election, believes the party badly misallocated its fundraising, misled donors and rewarded party operatives who propped up Biden’s image. "It was: ‘maintain this very obvious lie in return for access,’" Li recalled in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, referring to assertions that Biden was not experiencing cognitive decline. "And whoever maintained, whoever was most strident in propounding that lie got the most access. And whoever subverted it or dared to ask questions would see their access quickly diminish." Li herself would find her access completely cut off after she began questioning Biden’s physical ability to serve another four years as president. But before leaving, Li became a top operative and is now chronicling the months leading up to Biden's withdrawal from the race in her new book, "Unburdened." Her revelations include what then-Vice President Kamala Harris did with a historic, billion-dollar war chest. NANCY PELOSI DENIES KNOWING ABOUT BIDEN'S DECLINE, CLAIMS THOSE WHO KNEW 'SHOULD HAVE ACTED' For starters, Li believes that the numbers themselves weren’t what they appeared to be from the outside. "I sincerely believe it's a pyramid scheme," Li said. She explained how fundraisers would sometimes take credit for each other’s work. In some cases, top recruiters could effectively double-dip on work that their subordinates had done. "When you recruit somebody, you can claim up to $250,000 of what they raise," Li said. "In fact, you could poach other people's donors and move money around. And that is how some people reach like $10 million without actually raising a thing. It's like accounting gimmicks and machinations rather than real money. I know there were people who were double counted." As a top fundraiser for both Biden and Harris, Li worked closely with top donors, high-profile members of the party and the Democratic National Committee (DNC). Li described how she had a front-row seat for many of the party’s spending decisions. Li recounted that most of the Harris campaign's spending went through four large media contracting companies. These contractors, Li said, collected enormous fees and received over half a billion dollars. The companies that were listed in her book included Media Buying & Analytics, Gambit Strategies, Bully Pulpit Interactive and Dupont Circle Strategies. CARVILLE SHREDS DEMS' 2024 AUTOPSY, SAYS HARRIS CAMPAIGN WAS 'MOST INEFFECTIVE $2 BILLION EVER SPENT' "This tsunami of money represented about 70 percent of the campaign’s expenditures in the final days, enriching a handful of well-connected consultants while the broader effort collapsed," Li wrote. In interviews with Fox, Li described how the payments to the firms came partially as off-the-top fees. "The vast majority of the money raised went into TV ads. And so... You know, people talk about 10% for the big guy. Okay, but I actually think the bigger grift is 15% for the big grift for these media people. They get 15%, 15 points off of hundreds of millions of dollars. You can do the math," Li said. "The consultants get the money, the consultants that are hired by the campaign, and they're friends of the candidate or friends of Jen O’Malley-Dillon. It's a very incestuous process," Li said, referring to the Harris campaign chair. In addition to the media companies and the lucrative contracts they paid out, Li believes that the party focused too much on expenses that didn’t advance the campaign while, in her view, neglecting strategic opportunities. "$350,000 a night slapping her face in the Las Vegas sphere, spending that money on Gulfstream so they wouldn't have to fly commercial, spending it on Ritz-Carlton hotels. I mean, that definitely happened because the National Finance Committee was hosting its final meeting there. Spending its money on tote bags," Li said. "None of that in Philadelphia," she added, referring to the critical electoral center in Pennsylvania — a state that had been projected to be a pathway to victory in 2024. HARRIS BACKS RELEASING DNC'S 2024 ELECTION AUTOPSY DESPITE LEADERSHIP BURYING REPORT Part of what shocked Li was how brazen the party had been with the money she helped raise. She also expressed disbelief at the message the party spun to voters who had contributed their earnings in hopes of "saving democracy," a refrain Biden used to convince voters to side with him over President Donald Trump. "Some people forked over their life savings. Like people were liquidating their savings on the hope that they were saving the country. They absolutely did, and I truly believe that they donated $2.5 billion over seven weeks, not so much primarily because of Kamala's strength as a candidate, but rather their hatred for Trump and their fear of Trump," Li said. articles.title: Trump hails ‘very productive’ talks with China’s Xi Jinping
articles.summary: Xi says future of China-US ties ‘bright’ after state visit that included discussions about Iran and AI cooperation.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has hailed “very productive” talks with his counterpart Xi Jinping, which included a conversation on AI and the war in Iran, during the Chinese leader’s three-day state visit to Washington, DC.

When asked by reporters on Friday if the two leaders had discussed the war in Iran, Trump replied, “We did,” adding without providing details: “I think we’re going to do great.”

Trump also confirmed he will meet twice more this year with Xi: “We will be meeting again in November, in China, and then at the G20 in December, in Miami, Florida,” he said on Truth Social.

Trump added that this week’s meeting “was one of Friendship, Strength, and Success, for both China and the USA”.

During a tea ceremony at the White House on Friday, Xi – who was on his first visit to the US in more than a decade – said, “We invite the president and his wife to visit China,” also noting that the two leaders could have two further opportunities to meet this year.

Before departing at the end of his state visit, Xi told state-run Xinhua news agency that the future of China-US ties was “bright”.

Earlier on Friday, Trump wrote on Truth Social that “tremendous things will be happening” between the US and China, adding that his meetings with Xi were productive for both sides, emphasising the issue of artificial intelligence.

“[Xi] seemed to like calling the poorly and inaccurately named Artificial Intelligence to a far more accurate and important name, SUPER INTELLIGENCE. That would be ‘SUPER!’ Everyone last night agreed, also,” said the US president.

Trump told the United Nations General Assembly earlier this week that the US would rename artificial intelligence “super intelligence” in all US government documents.

Trump hosted a lavish state dinner on Thursday for Xi, which included high-profile guests like Amazon’s Jeff Bezos and Tesla head Elon Musk, who was seated at the main table alongside the Chinese and US presidents.

Despite being locked in a fierce strategic rivalry over AI, Trump and Xi have rebuffed recent calls from inside the US tech sector to slow the pace of development over concerns about controlling the rapidly advancing technology.

On Friday, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told Al Jazeera’s Alan Fisher that creating channels of communication on AI is one of the main challenges Washington and Beijing are seeking to overcome.

“I think with every government in the world right now, there isn’t a department of AI, and so there can be a question of who do you call when you have an issue,” Greer said, adding: “When I think about it, I think about the red zone between the Kremlin and the White House during the Cold War.”

Greer said another meeting on AI is planned within the next month between the representatives of both countries.

Separately, Greer told US media on Friday that the current talks did not cover the sale of a small amount of high-quality US-made chips requiring licences.

“These are the ⁠crown jewels of American technology. It’s the way we stay ahead in the race for superintelligence, or AI, and so those conversations … [are] not really happening in these negotiations,” Greer ‌said.

On the Iran war, David Perdue, the US ambassador to China, ‌told US-based business news network CNBC that Trump told Xi that direct or indirect support for Iran was “totally unacceptable”.

Perdue later told Fox News that China was already moving away from supporting Iran, saying, “That’s what the commitment is. They ⁠assured us yesterday they’re not doing that.”

Xi and Trump made a show of working to preserve harmony between the world’s two largest economies during the visit, though there were no major breakthroughs on issues such as trade or AI safety.

articles.title: Supreme Court allows Trump administration to use expanded database for potential voter purges
articles.summary: The Supreme Court permitted the Trump administration to expand a federal database containing citizenship information, as it encourages states to purge people from voter rolls.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Friday permitted the Trump administration to use an expanded federal database containing citizenship information, as the president encourages states to purge people from voter rolls. The justices, divided 6-3 on ideological lines with conservatives in the majority, granted an emergency request filed by the government after lower courts ruled that the Trump administration’s changes to the database were likely unlawful. Critics have said the data is unreliable and could lead to U.S. citizens being kicked off the voter rolls. But the court noted in its unsigned ruling that the National Voter Registration Act bars the broad purging of voter rolls in the weeks leading up to an election, which “limits the potential impact” of the decision this year. States can still make individualized queries about voters. On the broader legal questions raised in the case, the court said that federal law requires the government to respond to requests from states for information about citizenship. The lower court injunction “prevents the federal government from using the program it believes is best suited to the task,” the court said. In dissent, liberal Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote that the government had not done enough to show that the lower court ruling needed to be blocked. In her view, “the harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the Government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take,” she added. Various groups challenging the plan, led by the League of Women Voters, have argued that it violates several laws, including the Social Security Act and the Privacy Act. The Supreme Court decision “puts millions of Americans at risk for being unlawfully targeted by the administration’s unreliable voter purge database,” the groups said in a statement. Conservative who have backed the administration’s efforts to tighten voting laws, welcomed the decision. The ruling “just makes it easier for states to get federal citizenship data to help them clean up voter rolls,” Jason Snead, executive director of the Honest Elections Project, said in a statement. The Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements program, known as SAVE, was set up by Congress in 1986 so that government agencies could quickly determine someone’s immigration status when they applied for benefits like Social Security. The Trump administration expanded SAVE after President Donald Trump issued an executive order in March 2025 that required agencies to take steps to better ensure that only U.S. citizens vote in elections. The government expanded the database by adding information from the Social Security Administration, which enabled searches using Social Security numbers and allowed officials to do bulk searches. After states started putting their voter rolls through the newly expanded system, some local officials noticed mistakes; many of the flagged registrants were newly naturalized citizens, according to reporting from ProPublica and The Texas Tribune. Texas was one of the first states to put its full voter rolls — more than 18 million registrations — through the SAVE database last year. Just three people have been charged with voting illegally as a noncitizen. A federal judge blocked the Trump administration plan, with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit reaching the same conclusion. In court papers, Solicitor General D. John Sauer said that the district court’s ruling “threatens the integrity of upcoming elections” by preventing the government from responding to state requests to verify the citizenship of potential voters. Opponents argue the expanded database could force bureaucratic obligations on newly naturalized citizens who are asked to prove their citizenship after being flagged by the system. Noncitizen voting is extremely rare. All states are required to conduct voter roll list maintenance under federal law, and states already have processes to identify any noncitizens who do accidentally make it onto the voter rolls.

articles.title: Trump scores Supreme Court win in election integrity fight as states gain new voter roll tool
articles.summary: An order issued Friday by the Supreme Court temporarily allows the Trump administration to move forward with a mass voter verification system.
articles.body: An order issued Friday by the Supreme Court temporarily allows the Trump administration to move forward with a mass voter verification system. The emergency order allows states, for now, to use the Department of Homeland Security program, called Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, in their efforts to verify the eligibility of voters on their rolls. Because existing law blocks most states from systematically purging voters from their rolls within 90 days of an election, the immediate impact of Friday's order on the upcoming midterms is likely limited, the Associated Press reported. States' use of the SAVE program is voluntary. Norm Eisen, a senior fellow with Brookings, agreed that the Supreme Court's ruling was restrained. "Don't overreact to the SCOTUS SAVE database decision," Eisen wrote on X. "Page 6 of the decision makes clear that we are in the 90-day statutory window when mass changes can't be made to voter lists!" LIBERAL JUSTICE HAMMERS SUPREME COURT FOR FAST-TRACKING EMERGENCY DOCKET CASES The court’s order puts on hold a federal judge’s June ruling that had deemed the Republican administration’s recently revamped version of SAVE illegal. U.S. District Court Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan had blocked the use of the tool, saying it violated Americans’ privacy rights and could result in voters being wrongly removed from the rolls. A federal appeals court declined to pause Sooknanan's ruling, prompting the administration's appeal to the Supreme Court. The Trump administration moved to expand SAVE after the president signed an executive order directing the creation of a federal voter registration list and imposed new restrictions on eligibility for voting by mail as part of a broader effort to combat voter fraud. TRUMP REVIVES SUPREME COURT IMMIGRATION SHOWDOWN AFTER HOCHUL PARDON TORPEDOED FIRST CASE The SAVE program was created in 1986 under an immigration law mandating that DHS help federal, state and local agencies prevent government benefits from going to noncitizens. The Trump administration last year moved to significantly expand its search abilities. Since then, at least 67 million registrations have been scanned through the program, but critics, the AP says, worry it could end up purging valid voters from the rolls. Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was joined by Justices Elena Kagan and Sonia Sotomayor in dissenting. "In my view… the harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the Government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take," Jackson wrote in a dissenting opinion. "This imbalance, along with the Government’s improbable merits arguments, should have compelled the Court to deny the stay." But the majority pushed back on concerns that lawful voters could simply be removed from state voter rolls, noting that federal officials are required to contact individuals flagged by SAVE to seek additional information if their citizenship cannot be confirmed. The majority also noted that SAVE has long allowed federal, state and local agencies to verify citizenship and immigration status using records maintained by the Department of Justice, Department of Homeland Security and Department of State. "The Supreme Court’s order allows the federal government to share information in its possession concerning people’s apparent citizenship status to help election officials register eligible voters while preventing the improper addition of non-citizens to the registration rolls," Michael Morley, director of the Election Law Center at Florida State University, said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "The Court recognized Congress expressly endorsed such information sharing in 1996 amendments to federal immigration law." CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP The Supreme Court's stay is temporary, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit could still rule against the SAVE program, potentially sending the case back to the Supreme Court. Jason Snead, executive director of the Honest Elections Project, said the Supreme Court already "got it right." "The Trump Administration’s SAVE expansion just makes it easier for states to get federal citizenship data to help them clean up voter rolls. Once again, left-wing interests are doing everything they can to block states from verifying citizenship on the eve of a federal election, and for the second time in a week they have lost in court. This a major win for election integrity." Fox News' Shannon Bream, Bill Mears, Ashley J. DiMella and the Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Unearthed: El-Sayed called for repealing law that made sex without disclosing HIV status a felony
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed once called Michigan's HIV criminalization law "hateful" and "discriminatory," a stance now under scrutiny in his Senate race.
articles.body: Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed once called for repealing a Michigan law that made it a felony for people who knew they had HIV to have sex without first informing their partner — a position he is standing by eight years later as he campaigns in one of the nation's most competitive Senate races As he unsuccessfully ran for Michigan governor in 2018, El-Sayed repeatedly took aim at the law. The law carried a prison sentence of up to four years for people who knew they were HIV-positive and engaged in sexual penetration without first informing their partner of their HIV status. "You should not be criminalized for a disease. That is absolutely wrong. It’s hateful. It’s discriminatory, and we can, as a state, do better. You can count on me for that," El-Sayed said as he ran for governor. MICHIGAN STUDENT CONFRONTS EL-SAYED OVER IRAN STANCE Fast-forward eight years and El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and a former health director for Detroit-anchored Wayne County, is battling former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in the midterm race to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. The showdown in Michigan is a must hold for the Democrats as they try to win back control of the Senate from the GOP. As he ran for the 2018 Democratic gubernatorial nomination — a contest he lost to now-two-term Gov. Gretchen Whitmer — El-Sayed's campaign website stated, "Repeal HIV/AIDS criminalization laws and the exclusion of transgender Michiganders from state Medicaid." When asked in 2018 if he supported the decriminalization of HIV through legislation that would create two levels of misdemeanors, El-Sayed said at the time, "One of the big things that we have to recognize about HIV is that no disease can be illegal. The continuing forward of these laws on the books stigmatize people with the disease." SIX FORCES THAT COULD HELP REPUBLICANS DEFY HISTORY IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS Whitmer also supported changing the law, which dated to 1988, saying as she ran for governor, "It’s wrong to criminalize sickness, which is what this law has effectively done. It absolutely should be revisited." The law was reformed in early 2019, after passing a GOP-controlled legislature with broad bipartisan support. The revised statute limited the felony provisions to vaginal and anal intercourse involving an intent to transmit HIV or cases in which HIV was actually transmitted, reduced certain non-transmission offenses to misdemeanors and protected medically suppressed people from prosecution under the law's reckless-disregard provision. "Abdul supports the bipartisan reform bill that passed in 2019 through a Republican legislature that eliminated the discriminatory laws on the books," campaign spokesperson Roxie Richner told Fox News Digital. "As a public health professional, Abdul has fought to support programs that stem the spread of diseases, including HIV." Richner added that "the Trump administration has completely exacerbated this crisis by defunding the organizations and programs that do frontline care to prevent transmission and exposure in the first place. In the US Senate, Abdul will fight back against Donald Trump and RFK Jr’s attempts to dismantle our public health infrastructure and ensure all Americans have access to the care they need." DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB El-Sayed also stands by his past comments on fighting discrimination aimed at those with HIV. Last week, as he landed an endorsement from the Human Rights Campaign, a leading LGBTQ advocacy group, El-Sayed highlighted that if elected to the Senate, "I’ll fight to ensure every Michigander can live without discrimination and never have to wonder whether their rights will still be there tomorrow." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP El-Sayed, who narrowly edged more moderate Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens in August in a contentious primary that further exposed the rift between the party's left-wing and establishment factions, would become the nation’s first Muslim senator if elected. He has made support for "Medicare for all" a major component of his campaign. El-Sayed has also called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and has been a vocal critic of Israel during its war against Hamas, characterizing Israel’s actions in Gaza as "genocide" against Palestinians.

articles.title: Xi praises US state visit 'perfection' as Trump calls meetings 'very productive'
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said Friday that the U.S. and China have "made great strides" after meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House.
articles.body: Chinese President Xi Jinping praised the level of "perfection" on display during his state visit to the White House, and President Donald Trump said Friday the two world leaders had a "very productive" time in Washington. Trump, speaking to reporters as he and first lady Melania Trump hosted Xi and first lady of China Madame Peng Liyuan for tea at the White House, said, "We've had a tremendous visit from two spectacular people," and, "we've made great strides, very positive for both countries." "I want to thank the honorable president and the first lady for everything they've done for myself and my wife during this visit. Everything is down to the highest order of perfection," Xi responded through a translator. "And there is thought in every little detail. And it's greatly appreciated. XI CAPS TRUMP STATE VISIT WITH SYMBOLIC FINAL STOP BEFORE LEAVING WASHINGTON "The president and I are like two people that's charting the course for the great ship of China-U.S. relations," he continued. "When the president visited China in May, we agreed on the vision of building a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability. "This time, we've agreed to add new substance to it. That's the relationship, will be a constructive one of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity. So, from this, one can see that the prospects for this relationship will get more brighter." Xi, the leader of China’s ruling Communist Party, said he had two more opportunities to meet Trump this year, first at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting in China in November and then at the G20 Summit in December at Trump’s Doral resort in Miami, Florida. "We will see you, and we'll be speaking a lot. I think our farmers are going to be very happy," Trump said Friday. "A lot of very positive things happened. But America is very happy about this visit, and I'm sure China is very happy also. Great things for both countries. And it's been just very, very productive." TRUMP-XI REUNION COMES WITH UNFINISHED BUSINESS — AND A BIGGER BATTLE LOOMING Xi arrived in Washington Wednesday evening for a summit with Trump, four months after the two leaders reached a sweeping agreement that included Chinese commitments on rare earths, agricultural purchases, trade and investment. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Trump hailed that agreement as a breakthrough for American farmers, manufacturers and workers. But the latest talks unfolded during uneven progress on commitments involving rare-earth minerals, agricultural and commercial purchases, trade and investment, while key disputes over tariffs, advanced technology, artificial intelligence, intellectual property and Taiwan remain unresolved. "President Xi and Madam Peng have just left D.C., heading for China. The meeting was one of Friendship, Strength, and Success, for both China and the U.S.A.," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Much has been, and will be, accomplished. I look forward to our next meeting!" Fox News Digital’s Ashley J. DiMella and Peter D’Abrosca contributed to this report.

articles.title: Jack Smith to testify before Senate Judiciary next week
articles.summary: Former special counsel Jack Smith will testify before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday, his second appearance before Congress as they probe his investigation into President Trump. Smith led a team of Justice Department investigators and ultimately determined he would bring charges against Trump in the Mar-a-Lago documents case and another related to the president’s…
articles.body:
Former special counsel Jack Smith will testify before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday, his second appearance before Congress as they probe his investigation into President Trump.

Smith led a team of Justice Department investigators and ultimately determined he would bring charges against Trump in the Mar-a-Lago documents case and another related to the president’s actions on Jan. 6, 2021.

Smith will sit across from Judiciary Committee Chair Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), one of Congress’s most vocal critics of the prosecutor’s work.

Grassley’s team has titled the hearing “Oversight of Jack Smith’s Abuse of Authority and the Targeting of Republicans.”

He has repeatedly released documents he has obtained about Smith’s investigation, including toll records showing that Smith reviewed call logs of some senators who spoke with Trump on Jan. 6. Smith did not have access to the content of the calls.

Democrats framed the hearing as a chance for Smith to defend a well-founded investigation.

“Donald Trump spent months spreading the Big Lie and pressuring election officials & Members of Congress to help overturn the 2020 election. Jack Smith investigated this criminal effort. Finally on Tuesday, Mr. Smith will be able to tell the Senate Judiciary Committee his story,” Senate Judiciary Democrats wrote on the social platform X.

Smith testified before the House Judiciary Committee in January.

In closed-door testimony in December, Smith defended bringing the cases.

“If asked whether to prosecute a former president based on the same facts today, I would do so regardless of whether the president was a Republican or Democrat,” Smith said in his prepared remarks.

“The decision to bring charges against President Trump was mine, but the basis for those charges rests entirely with President Trump and his actions, as alleged in the indictments returned by grand juries in two different districts,” he added.

articles.title: Senate approves legislation targeted at pilot, air traffic control mental health guidance
articles.summary: The Senate passed two bills Thursday aimed at removing barriers for pilots and air traffic controllers seeking mental health treatment, as well as reducing stigma surrounding these conditions. Sponsored by Sens. John Hoeven (R-N.D.) and Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), respectively, both pieces of legislation passed in the upper chamber by unanimous consent. The first act, which…
articles.body:
The Senate passed two bills Thursday aimed at removing barriers for pilots and air traffic controllers seeking mental health treatment, as well as reducing stigma surrounding these conditions.

Sponsored by Sens. John Hoeven (R-N.D.) and Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), respectively, both pieces of legislation passed in the upper chamber by unanimous consent.

The first act, which Hoeven introduced , would require the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to issue guidance encouraging pilots and air traffic controllers struggling with mental health issues to seek treatment. It would also provide “enhanced” training for aviation medical examiners on how to address these conditions.

The bill honors John A. Hauser , an aviation student from Chicago who took his own life in 2021 while attending the University of North Dakota.

“Our nation faces a severe shortage of qualified pilots and air traffic controllers, while bureaucratic delays and outdated processes at the FAA keep these professionals from working for prolonged periods when they seek mental health care,” Hoeven said in a statement after senators passed the package.

The other bill, brought forth by Duckworth, seeks to boost transparency around available medications for aviation industry employees.

This legislation, titled the Aviation Medication Transparency Act of 2026 , would direct the FAA to create and annually update a list of medications that can be safely prescribed to pilots and air traffic controllers.

“Our aviation system depends on the well-being of our pilots and air traffic controllers, who operate under an immense amount of stress,” Duckworth said in a statement. “Their careers should never be threatened because they weren’t properly informed about which medications they’re allowed to take, or simply sought the mental health care they need.”

Both bills now head to the House for consideration.

Earlier this year, the FAA issued new guidance encouraging pilots and air traffic controllers to seek counseling, as well as other mental health services. The Hill has reached out to the agency for comment on the Senate’s approval of these two bills.

articles.title: Federal illegal voting arrest becomes latest flashpoint in Sherrill's battles with Trump administration
articles.summary: New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill faces new pressure after ICE and the FBI arrested a Senegalese national accused of voting illegally since 2018.
articles.body: Federal law enforcement arrested a Senegalese immigrant in New Jersey accused of illegally voting in multiple elections, injecting a new flashpoint into Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill's escalating fights with Washington over immigration enforcement and election integrity. The case comes as Washington and Trenton battle over immigration enforcement and election administration, with the Trump administration challenging Sherrill over state policies affecting federal law enforcement while also pressing New Jersey for access to its voter rolls. Sanata Coulibaly, a Senegalese national, was arrested when DHS and FBI agents jointly executed a criminal warrant in Hudson County, which stretches from West New York to Bayonne across the Hudson River from Manhattan. FOUR NONCITIZENS CHARGED WITH ILLEGALLY VOTING IN 2020, 2022 AND 2024 FEDERAL ELECTIONS IN NEW JERSEY "This alien from Senegal has been charged with procurement of citizenship or naturalization unlawfully and voting by an alien after allegedly voting in three general elections in New Jersey," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said. "Sanctuary politicians can try to claim that this kind of voter fraud isn’t happening, but it’s very real and is a serious threat to our country." WATCH: TRUMP DOJ VOWS TO PURSUE ‘EVERY SINGLE’ VOTING VIOLATION AFTER NJ ROLL SHOCKER Mullin said DHS and the Trump administration would continue efforts to protect election integrity. The arrest comes after Sherrill revealed in July that a software error in New Jersey's motor vehicle system had improperly registered roughly 6,600 people who identified themselves as noncitizens. The state later determined that fewer than 400 of those newly registered because of the error had voted. After that revelation, New Jersey resisted federal demands to turn over voter rolls while pursuing its own investigation. Fox News Digital reached out to Sherrill for comment. According to the criminal complaint, Coulibaly cast ballots in the November 2018 midterm election, the July 2020 primary, the November 2020 general election and the 2024 general election while she was not a U.S. citizen. Coulibaly registered through a paper application submitted to the Hudson County superintendent of elections in Jersey City, falsely certifying that she was a U.S. citizen, the complaint said. She first came to the U.S. from Senegal on a B-1 nonimmigrant visa in approximately 1993 and later became a lawful permanent resident, according to the Justice Department. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Prosecutors allege Coulibaly later applied for U.S. citizenship and falsely stated on her N-400 naturalization application that she had never registered to vote or voted in a federal election. articles.title: New Jersey Lt Gov Dale Caldwell resigns after sexual harassment investigation
articles.summary: New Jersey Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell resigned after an investigation substantiated sexual harassment and ethics violations, Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced Friday.
articles.body: Democrat New Jersey Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell resigned Friday after an independent investigation substantiated sexual harassment and ethics violations against him, Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced. "The investigation found that the lieutenant governor failed to uphold the responsibilities of his office, and he demonstrated a pattern of behavior that does not meet the standards of this administration," Sherrill said during a news conference in Trenton. articles.title: Bill Clinton: ‘There were lots of times when I wanted to ban the White House press corps’
articles.summary: Former President Clinton rebuked President Trump’s attempted ban of three outlets from the White House last week, saying during his presidency, “There were lots of times when I wanted to ban the White House press corps.” “I got news for the people who work in the White House today. There were lots of times when…
articles.body:
Former President Clinton rebuked President Trump’s attempted ban of three outlets from the White House last week, saying during his presidency, “There were lots of times when I wanted to ban the White House press corps.”

“I got news for the people who work in the White House today. There were lots of times when I wanted to ban the White House press corps,” he said at the Clinton Global Initiative 2026 summit . “And there’s a reason we have a constitution. Because none of us are immune from being pissed off.”

“But I’m glad I never did, and I’m glad I couldn’t. And these people shouldn’t. The law should be what it is,” the former president added.

His wife, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, called the ban against the three outlets “deeply disturbing,” in a Tuesday interview with The Washington Post .

“That is part of the give-and-take in not just politics, but democracy,” she said, continuing that such a ban is “unfortunately what authoritarians do.”

On Thursday, a judge ruled in favor of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, ordering the White House to reverse its ban. Journalists from the three outlets were initially denied entry into the White House following the court’s ruling but were given access later in the day.

MS NOW and CNN journalists also reported Thursday they were denied access to the state dinner arrival at the White House during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the U.S., which was a precredentialed event.

Former President Obama has also weighed in on the controversy, stating at an event Monday night that he believed this issue “should not be a partisan issue” as this “should be something that rises above partisanship.”

Obama said he was not surprised by the ban, and it was as if “the president of the United States can’t take some criticism,” according to CNN .

“You do not have, as far as I can tell, any substantial group of Republicans who are standing up and saying, ‘No, you can’t do that, because we don’t want, if there’s a Democratic president, to be banning Fox News,’ or whatever other outlets that are going off on Democratic presidents,” he said.

articles.body: New Jersey Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell has resigned from his position following an investigation that found he violated state ethics and harassment policy, Gov. Mikie Sherrill said Friday at a press conference. “He submitted his resignation to me this afternoon, which I accepted,” Sherrill said. Caldwell was not present at the announcement. On Thursday, Sherrill urged Caldwell’s resignation after releasing a report summarizing the findings of a probe of his behavior conducted by a law firm hired by the state, which found evidence that he violated ethics rules by committing sexual harassment. In a statement Thursday, Sherrill said that Caldwell, a fellow Democrat, “engaged in serious, repeated violations of state policy and failed to uphold the responsibilities of his office. I’m calling for his resignation and giving him until tomorrow to do so.” Caldwell’s resignation, she added, “is necessary and in the best interest of New Jersey residents.” Investigators said in the 61-page report that they found credible evidence that Caldwell violated workplace policy “in his conduct by commenting to a female staffer that young women want ‘young sperm.’” They also found he violated an ethics code and code of conduct “when he brought guests to ticketed events without payment or reimbursement” and “when he sought to obtain a promotion for a state employee with whom he had a romantic relationship.” Lawyers for Caldwell, who has denied the allegations, said in a statement Thursday night that they “strongly disputed the three findings in the investigation,” as its conclusions “go further than the evidence supports.” “This unnecessarily protracted and one-sided process lacked the requisite due process that should be afforded every citizen of this state,” said Caldwell’s attorney Thomas Calcagni. Calcagni didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment Friday. On Friday, Sherrill pushed back on Calcagni’s criticism of the investigation, saying: “I think it’s very thorough. It lays out exactly what the investigation looked into.” She added that Caldwell’s own statements were included in the report, saying, “So, obviously he was fully involved in this as well.” Sherrill also defended having Caldwell step in as acting governor on several occasions after the investigation began, saying, “As a former federal prosecutor, it is important to me that everyone have a fair hearing.” “Once I saw those complaints, once I saw the findings of that investigation, I acted quickly and asked for the resignation of the lieutenant governor,” Sherrill said. The governor said her demand that Caldwell step down is part of her efforts to dismantle a culture that ignores victims. “There has been a culture in Trenton, probably since the birth of our nation, to sweep this under the rug,” Sherrill said. “That is not the kind of government I’m running. When I say there is a culture change taking place, I mean it. This is part of it.” New Jersey state Assembly Speaker Craig Coughlin, a Democrat, applauded Sherrill for her “commitment to hold public officials to the highest standards.” “Following an independent investigation, Lieutenant Governor Dale Caldwell was right to resign from office today,” Coughlin said in a statement. “We must ensure the work of governing is uninterrupted and that serving the people of New Jersey remains a top priority.” Caldwell was also serving as New Jersey’s secretary of state, an office that oversees elections. Sherrill said Friday that the state’s acting comptroller, Shirley Emehelu, would become acting secretary of state with just weeks to go until the midterm elections. “Shirley is a veteran of the U.S. Department of Justice and the New Jersey Attorney General’s Office,” Sherrill said. “She has the judgment to run these elections and the strength to stand up to Trump’s attacks on voting.” The lieutenant governor’s duties also include filling in for the governor when she leaves the state. Sherrill said that until a new lieutenant governor is in place, there is “an order of command” for who would step in for her during any absence, beginning with the state Senate president. Under New Jersey law, the lieutenant governor must be replaced within 45 days of the position becoming vacant. Sherrill said she would “certainly” make a permanent appointment within that time frame but does not plan on naming an acting lieutenant governor in the meantime. “We will be making sure with our chief counsel that we’re following the rules,” Sherrill said. “This is a little bit of a new area for New Jersey, so we’re going to ensure that we get legal opinions and follow the process there.”

articles.body: En la previa del compromiso amistoso entre Colombia y México en Baltimore (Estados Unidos), el director técnico de la 'Tricolor', Néstor Lorenzo, se refirió al homenaje y partido de despedida que se contempla para James Rodríguez, tras confirmarse el retiro del talentoso volante cucuteño del combinado nacional. El estratega argentino dejó claro que, aunque la decisión final recae sobre el futbolista, tanto el cuerpo técnico como los directivos de la Federación Colombiana de Fútbol están totalmente dispuestos a habilitar una ventana internacional para rendirle el homenaje que merece. “No he hablado, eso es una decisión de James. Es un jugador activo y él decidirá cuándo y dónde será su despedida. La Selección Colombia seguramente estará abierta en estas ventanas, en estas fechas FIFA de amistosos, para conversar esa posibilidad”, declaró Lorenzo en rueda de prensa. Aunque la decisión sigue estando en manos del ex número '10', la posibilidad más firme que se contempla en el entorno de la Selección es la ventana FIFA del mes de noviembre. El escenario elegido para este hipotético homenaje sería el Estadio Pascual Guerrero de Cali, donde el volante podría vestir por última vez la camiseta amarilla ante la afición colombiana, siguiendo un modelo similar al que implementó Argentina con Lionel Messi en el Estadio Monumental. El estratega nacional también abordó cómo afrontará el equipo esta nueva etapa sin su principal referente y capitán en el terreno de juego, enfatizando en que no se busca un reemplazo individual directo, sino un ajuste en el funcionamiento colectivo: Lorenzo destacó que futbolistas con la categoría de James Rodríguez o Juan Fernando Quintero no abundan, especialmente en su capacidad para leer el partido y ejecutar jugadas decisivas. “La categoría de James, de Juanfer y esos jugadores no la tiene cualquiera. A lo mejor hay muchos jugadores con calidad, pero la adaptación a la Selección hace que tenga que decidir el momento de cómo y cuándo ejecutar alguna jugada magistral o un pase. Vamos a seguir con la misma idea, tratando de mejorar” Ante las ausencias de figuras habituales, el cuerpo técnico busca consolidar el nuevo liderazgo dentro del camerino. “Nosotros al equipo le damos las herramientas para saber dónde nos conviene recuperar, de qué manera, por dónde nos conviene salir jugando y luego ellos tienen que decidir dentro del campo” La Selección Colombia continúa así su preparación en territorio norteamericano para afrontar sus compromisos internacionales, mientras la afición permanece a la espera de la confirmación oficial para el último baile de una de las máximas leyendas del fútbol colombiano.

articles.title: McConnell, Cornyn join letter questioning Trump invite to Putin
articles.summary: A group of senators, including seven Republicans, sent an open letter to President Trump on Friday to express “serious concern” and press him to explain why he invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to attend the Group of 20 Leaders’ Summit in Miami later this year amid Russia’s war with Ukraine. “Given President Putin’s continued actions…
articles.body:
A group of senators, including seven Republicans, sent an open letter to President Trump on Friday to express “serious concern” and press him to explain why he invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to attend the Group of 20 Leaders’ Summit in Miami later this year amid Russia’s war with Ukraine.

“Given President Putin’s continued actions against the Ukrainian people and U.S. national security interests, we urge you to reconsider granting President Putin the stature and legitimacy to appear in the United States as a world leader at the G20 Leaders’ Summit,” the senators wrote.

Such a letter is common from Democrats, in this case the opposite party to the president. But the handful of Republicans who signed on went beyond the usual Trump critics in the GOP: Sens. Mitch McConnell (Ky.), John Cornyn (Texas), Roger Wicker (Miss.), Jerry Moran (Kan.), Thom Tillis (N.C.), John Curtis (Utah) and Alan Armstrong (Okla.).

Their support on the letter, which urged Trump to rescind any such invitation to Putin and any other sanctioned Russian officials, demonstrates how Senate Republicans generally still support Ukraine in its war with Russia and some have become more willing to push back on Trump amid his low approval rating.

The letter also cited the recently passed Russia-Iran sanctions bill, named for former Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), who was one of the staunchest defenders of Ukraine in the Senate before his death in July. That bill increased sanctions on Russia, hoping to squeeze it economically as its aggression in Ukraine continues four years after invading that country.

But Russian officials have still been present at official meetings around the U.S. in recent months, the senators said, even those who are already sanctioned.

“It is troubling that, despite being sanctioned, these individuals have been given access to participate in G20 forums hosted in the United States,” the senators wrote. “The G20 is intended to foster international cooperation on critical issues including finance, trade and global economic stability. As Russia continues its war against Ukraine and refuses to agree to a just and lasting peace agreement, its government should not be afforded a business-as-usual treatment alongside other nations at G20 events.”

Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Wicker, the chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee, sent a similar letter to administration officials in April questioning Russian delegates’ participation in meetings with members of Congress and executive branch officials.

The G20 Leaders’ Summit is an annual gathering of 19 sovereign nations’ representatives from across the world. The countries together represent 85 percent of the gross world product and more than half of the world’s population.

Trump is hosting it in December at his resort in Miami.

articles.title: New Jersey lieutenant governor resigns after sexual harassment accusation
articles.summary: Investigation determined Dale Caldwell violated state ethics rules and engaged in harassing behavior
articles.body:
Dale Caldwell, the lieutenant governor of New Jersey, resigned from his position on Friday, after the release of a report accusing him of sexually harassing a female staffer, among other ethics violations.

New Jersey's governor, Mikie Sherrill, announced on Friday afternoon that Caldwell had submitted his resignation to her earlier in the day.

The decision by Caldwell, 66, came one day after Sherrill called on him to step down after an investigation determined he violated state ethics rules and engaged in behavior that constituted sexual harassment.

The 61-page report said it found credible evidence that Caldwell made romantic advances toward a female staffer's friend, tried to secure a promotion for his girlfriend and gave tickets to personal guests without reimbursement.

The New Jersey Globe was the first to report on Caldwell's resignation.

Thomas Calcagni, a lawyer for Caldwell, said in a statement they would "continue to forcefully challenge the report".

"Dr Caldwell's resignation, submitted to put an end to the targeted campaign to discredit his character, does not in any way diminish our outrage concerning the investigative process and its specious findings," Calcagni said. "Counsel is fully exploring all legal remedies to ensure a true, balanced, and unbiased record."

Sherrill, a Democrat, said she would appoint the state's acting comptroller, Shirley Emehelu, as the acting lieutenant governor.

"We can no longer tolerate the culture of silence, sweeping things under the rug or kicking cans down the road," Sherrill said Friday at press conference in Trenton, the state capital. "New Jerseyans deserve fairness and they deserve accountability."

The change-up comes just weeks before midterm elections, which the lieutenant governor is responsible for overseeing.

The New Jersey governor initiated an investigation into Caldwell in May after receiving an anonymous letter that accused him of "bringing uninvited female guests to events while traveling using taxpayer funds" and "hitting on women at functions".

Ultimately, investigators concluded that aspects of the allegations were credible.

In one instance, investigators said Caldwell made a romantic advance toward a female staffer's friend and then made a "derogatory or demeaning reference" about women after his advances were rebuffed.

Caldwell allegedly told the staffer that women like them were ambitious and successful and needed a man in a position to help them, "but you young women are looking for young sperm".

Investigators also found that Caldwell advocated for the promotion of his girlfriend, a state employee, to a "senior leadership position". Caldwell acknowledged that he did not disclose the nature of his relationship with the state employee until he was confronted.

Caldwell had pushed for his girlfriend's promotion, even after being informed he was under investigation. Ultimately, she did not get the promotion and no longer works in state government.

Credible evidence also determined Caldwell brought at least three personal guests, including his girlfriend, to ticketed events, in his capacity as lieutenant governor, without advance authorization or payment.

After Sherrill announced the report's findings and called for Caldwell to resign, it was unclear whether or not he would step down.

As lieutenant governor, Caldwell was also serving as New Jersey's secretary of state, who is the chief elections officer.

With just 39 days until the midterm elections, Sherrill said she was tapping Emehelu to ensure "all eligible New Jerseyans can make their voices heard".

"Shirley is a veteran of the US Department of Justice and the New Jersey attorney general's office. She has the judgment to run these elections and the strength to stand up to Trump's attacks on voting," Sherrill added.

Sherrill has 45 days to name a permanent replacement for Caldwell.

New Jersey Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell (D) resigned Friday following calls to step down from his position after an investigation found that he had violated state ethics and harassment policies.

Caldwell allegedly made a sexually charged comment to a staffer and twice attempted to secure a promotion for a state employee with whom he had a romantic relationship.

Sherrill gave Caldwell until Friday to resign from his position, saying he had “engaged in serious, repeated violations of state policy and failed to uphold the responsibilities of his office.”

“The Lieutenant Governor’s resignation is necessary and in the best interest of New Jersey residents,” she said.

Among the incidents detailed in the report, investigators said Caldwell made a romantic advance toward the female friend of a staffer. After the woman rejected him, Caldwell allegedly told the staffer, “You young women are looking for young sperm.”

Caldwell, who also oversees the state’s elections as secretary of state, denied making the remark, but investigators said they did not find his denial credible.

His attorney, Thomas Calcagni, disputed the investigation’s findings Thursday, arguing that the process was one-sided and did not give Caldwell a sufficient opportunity to respond to the allegations.

Sherrill announced Friday that acting state Comptroller Shirley Emehelu will take over as acting secretary of state, just weeks before the midterm elections.

With the lieutenant governor’s office now vacant, under New Jersey’s succession rules, the state Senate president — in this case, state Sen. Nicholas Scutari (D) — is next in line to assume the governor’s duties when Sherrill is out of state or otherwise unable to serve.

articles.title: Anti-Trump attorney: ‘Don’t overreact’ to Supreme Court voter database decision
articles.summary: Norm Eisen, a former White House ethics lawyer and frequent critic of President Trump, urged Americans not to “overreact” after the Supreme Court’s Friday ruling permitting the administration to move forward with its new immigration database ahead of the midterm elections. In an emergency ruling, the high court found that the Trump administration could proceed…
articles.body:
Norm Eisen, a former White House ethics lawyer and frequent critic of President Trump, urged Americans not to “overreact” after the Supreme Court’s Friday ruling permitting the administration to move forward with its new immigration database ahead of the midterm elections.

In an emergency ruling , the high court found that the Trump administration could proceed with its plans to allow states to use this overhauled online system to search for ineligible voters.

Eisen noted that the majority opinion acknowledged the provision of the National Voter Registration Act that bars states from implementing systemic voter removal programs within 90 days of an election.

However, the justices noted that limited “individualized inquiries” could still proceed.

“Page 6 of the decision makes clear that we are in the 90 day statutory window when mass changes can’t be made to voter lists!” Eisen wrote on social media . “It’s a s‑‑‑ decision for the reasons the 3 dissenters say but we can deal w/it.”

The decision, which was unsigned and did not provide a vote count, was opposed by the court’s three liberal justices. It overturns a lower-court ruling that prevented the Trump administration from distributing this new system to states.

“The order below prevents the Federal Government from using the program it believes is best suited to the task,” the court wrote in its majority opinion.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson authored the 12-page dissenting opinion, joined by Justices Elena Kagan and Sonia Sotomayor.

“In my view, however, the harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the Government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take,” Jackson wrote.

Their presence alongside field marshals, volunteer coordinators and campaign organizers showed an operation with designated personnel responsible for recruitment, messaging, crowd movement and event logistics. Nearby, towering over many of the protesters, Taher Dahleh, an organizer with another partner of the People’s Forum — the Palestinian Youth Movement — moved through the crowd, grabbing a Winstone Blue cigarette from another activist, directing demonstrators and coordinating the march. He has been a familiar presence at anti-Israel demonstrations since Oct. 7, 2023, regularly hosting volunteer meetings on Monday nights at the People’s Forum for a campaign called "Shut It Down For Palestine." During the "March on Washington to Let Gaza Live!" that People’s Forum co-organized in November 2025, Dahleh slammed "tech companies" for allegedly contributing to the "slaughter" of Palestinians by selling services to the government of Israel. Between late 2023 and late 2024, far-left nonprofit WesPac Foundation Inc. gave Palestinian Youth Movement $1 million through its nonprofit fiscal sponsor, Honor the Earth, according to tax filings. Records show it’s received funds from several other sources over the years. The Palestinian Youth Movement still shares a post on its Facebook page from years ago, quoting a young Palestinian killed after murdering three Israelis: "You who possess arms and bullets, remember that there is an enemy so that you may put your bullets in their bodies, not the bodies of your own people." Dahleh didn’t respond to a request for comment. HOUSE PANEL SUBPOENAS 3 LEFT-WING GROUPS IN PROBE OF $39M TIED TO MARXIST TYCOON NEVILLE SINGHAM The protest followed a familiar playbook that Evans, De Los Santos, Fuleihan, Dahleh, Chung, the People’s Forum and the Singham network have used since Oct. 7, 2023, to mobilize students at Columbia University, launch a campus encampment and storm Grand Central Terminal. Since then, the same constellation of communist, socialist and anti-war groups has repeatedly turned out for protests over Israel, ICE, the Trump administration, the war against the Islamic Republic of Iran, the arrest of Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro and other political flashpoints — including protests against U.S. data centers, American AI, and U.S. technology companies like Palantir Technologies, Microsoft and Google. This time, Dahleh and People’s Forum field marshals led the activists from the steps of the public library on Fifth Avenue to E. 42nd Street, where they headed eastbound toward the United Nations past Grand Central Station. Inside the crowd, the network’s social media operation made the march seem like a spontaneous display of mass public anger. At 5:20 p.m., with the march still in force, People’s Forum posted a tightly-cropped video on X, showing demonstrators streaming below flapping American flags with a caption celebrating a "massive crowd of protesters taking to the streets demanding war criminal Netanyahu be brought to justice! Free Palestine!" However, outside the limited mile-long path of the march, New Yorkers went about their ordinary days. The repeated appearance of the same organizations, leaders, signs, sound systems, wagons and protest infrastructure rolling through the streets of New York City revealed the professional organizing system operating behind the scenes, not a "massive crowd." WATCH: Neville Roy Singham’s wife Jodie Evans appears at anti-Israel protest, denies he funds protest efforts Jodie Evans takes center stage On E. 42nd Street, Evans — Singham’s wife and a central figure in the network surrounding the People’s Forum and other Singham-funded organizations — smiled widely as she kept step with the activists, marching behind the bright yellow-and-black signs marked "Party for Socialism and Liberation." Evans marched with CodePink activists behind a large "STOP ARMING ISRAEL" banner and carried a poster depicting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as "WANTED" for "GENOCIDE." Evans stood out in trademark CodePink colors, wearing an oversized fuchsia hat, pink peace-sign earrings, dark glasses, a pink-and-white keffiyeh and a shirt reading "I ♥ Palestinian Human Rights." Her appearance placed a member of the financier’s immediate family directly in the middle of the protest activity his money has helped sustain. When Fox News Digital asked her about her husband’s funding for nonprofits leading anti-Israel protests, she didn’t answer the question directly and responded, "He’s not been in the United States for six-and-a-half years." When asked about his position on the protests, she answered: "He supports stopping a genocide, you bet." Evans laughed off questions about Singham backing the Chinese Communist Party. In a video that Fox News Digital unearthed, Singham stood at the Golden Tulip Hotel in Shanghai during a November 2025 conference and expressed support for "a new world order that is based on multilateralism that President Xi and the CPC [Communist Party of China] and China have proposed." LAWMAKERS THROW OUT 'TROJAN HORSE' ACTIVISTS THEY SAY ARE ENGAGED IN AMERICAN SUBVERSION Evans denied allegations from lawmakers on the House Foreign Affairs Committee that the Singham network acts as a "Trojan horse" for the Chinese Communist Party, calling them "a lot of lies." "We're not doing anything wrong. So it's a lot of ‘alleging,’ and we're very honest about what we do: protesting every day," she said. "That's what we do. And that's what I've done for 55 years." She got visibly agitated on the topic of China. "China is not our enemy!" she said. "That's the message. You know what? I've been going to China for six and a half years. I can't talk about China. It's complex. I don't understand it. I'm just trying to learn about it. So it's not about China. It's about the United States not using our tax dollars to go to war on China. There's never an excuse to go to war on people." The protest was also packaged for online amplification. During the march, Zoe Alexandra, news editor of BreakThrough News, moved through the crowd conducting interviews, pulling Danaka Katovich, national co-director of CodePink, away from Evans’ CodePink contingent for a chat. BreakThrough later posted a branded one-minute, 21-second video on X under the headline: "Thousands protest…" Singham gave $1.098 million to Breakthrough BT Media Inc., which operates BreakThrough News, according to tax filings. SINGHAM-LINKED NONPROFITS FIGHT HOUSE SUBPOENAS, ACCUSE LAWMAKERS OF MCCARTHY-ERA ‘WITCH HUNT’ The protest featured black-and-white keffiyehs, a torched effigy of Netanyahu, bloodied cardboard imagery of Netanyahu and Arabic chants declaring that "Israel will be Arab." Critics say the slogans and imagery go beyond criticism of Israeli policy, invoking violent resistance and portraying the elimination of Israel as a political objective. To close out the protest near the United Nations, a leader from the Singham network manned the pop-up stage with a black-and-white keffiyeh over his shoulders, his arms tightly crossed, as speakers blasted the U.S. and Israel. As their last speaker, organizers returned to another leader from the People's Forum, Tajee Bounds, who serves as membership, events and volunteer coordinator. A graduate of Columbia University, Bounds was in the middle of the campus’s first encampment in April 2024 with People's Forum organizers when he stood, holding a banner and yelling along with a chant: "Up, up with liberation! Down, down with occupation!" The Columbia Spectator posted a video with his proclamation. Packing up the protest "Glory, glory to our martyrs," an activist chanted, before Bounds took the microphone at 6:31 p.m. to lead the crowd in a chant: "Gaza! Gaza! You will rise!" At 7:01 p.m., People’s Forum activists began rolling away their wagon full of yellow-and-black signs, set upside down, declaring, "ARREST WAR CRIMINAL BENJAMIN NETANYAHU!" Bounds and others began breaking down their stage and speaker system. HOW CODEPINK CO-FOUNDER MEDEA BENJAMIN'S FAMILY FOUNDATION BECAME A MAJOR FUNDER OF LEFT-WING ACTIVIST GROUPS For a dramatic backdrop, the protest moved west on 42nd Street to Times Square, like so many protests have ended before. There, CodePink's Benjamin, Evans' fellow co-founder and a guest at Singham and Evans’ wedding in 2017, created a video for Instagram with herself standing in front of the protesters wearing a black-and-white keffiyeh scarf and narrating to the camera the day's events: "These protests against Netanyahu and the Israeli regime have been going on since 10 a.m. All day long! Now it’s nighttime!" CodePink’s message throughout the video repeated the mantra of the day’s protest: "FROM THE RIVER TO THE SEA PALESTINE WILL BE FREE." The videos presented the demonstration as a spontaneous eruption of grassroots anger. But the footage was the product of the same operation it portrayed: professional organizers supplied the signs, sound equipment, rolling carts, stage and coordinated messaging, while BreakThrough News, People’s Forum and CodePink activists recorded and distributed footage from the event. The sequence created a feedback loop in which organizers built the spectacle, captured it on video and circulated the images as evidence of the movement’s scale and momentum. After the Times Square theater, foot soldiers for the People’s Forum rolled their wagon back onto W. 42nd Street, past the Port Authority and a McDonald’s on Eighth Avenue, with their trademark bright yellow-and-black signs. Others carried the bloodied cardboard imagery of Netanyahu and other protest paraphernalia. They ended up at the hub of the anti-Israel activist, the headquarters of the People’s Forum on W. 34th Street, carrying signs past books by communist leader Karl Marx and other ideologues. Inside the People’s Forum's large meeting hall, Chung, organizing director of the People’s Forum, awaited the returning protesters. De Los Santos greeted them at the door, stepping outside to tell Fox News Digital that he was proud of the group’s work leading the anti-Israel protests for the past three years. "We organize protests. What is wrong or illegal about that?" De Los Santos said, as his workers drew the shades on the People’s Forum. He also declared proudly, "Yeah, I am a communist."
