articles.title: WATCH: DHS issues stark warning after 300 ‘hostile’ cartel drones detected at southern border
articles.summary: The Department of Homeland Security warned cartels their drones are failing as 378 were detected at the southern border in just over one month.
articles.body: The Department of Homeland Security issued a stark warning after more than 300 cartel drones were detected along the southern border in just over a month. According to the Department of War, 378 cartel drones were detected at the southern border between Aug. 22 and Thursday. Of those, 75 drones were turned back, 15 were engaged and one was captured. Fox News Digital previously reported that the War Department’s Joint Task Force – Southern Border took down "approximately" 100 suspected cartel drones in August alone. In response to the threat, the Department of War and DHS are increasing their use of drone detection and interception tools along the southern border. The agencies are also working with private companies to develop technology to counter the increased presence of cartel drones. In a statement posted on X, DHS wrote that "hostile surveillance of American personnel ends here." EXCLUSIVE: TRUMP’S CBP AXES BIDEN-ERA POLICY ALLOWING PRIVATE GIFTS FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS IN FEDERAL CUSTODY "To the Cartels," DHS wrote, "Your drones are failing, your tactics are being exposed, and you have no advantage. @CBP and @DeptofWar will keep taking them down." In an interview with Fox News, Jeffrey Stalnaker, deputy chief patrol agent for Border Patrol, said cartels primarily use drones for reconnaissance during drug and human smuggling operations rather than for smuggling. Cartels previously sent lookouts to monitor Border Patrol agents and other U.S. personnel but now use drones to watch from overhead. "They’re watching when our soldiers and our agents are coming into the field, where they’re working, and then that allows them to plan how they’re going to send individuals north from Mexico into the United States illegally, trying to circumvent us between the ports of entry," he explained. Federal officials told Fox News that U.S. anti-drone measures at the southern border have succeeded so far, but cartel drone tactics are rapidly evolving. Some cartel drones are known to be used for lethal purposes, but officials said those have not yet been encountered at the border. For the past three weeks, the U.S. military has been conducting exercises in the desert outside Yuma, Arizona, testing new anti-drone gear ranging from guns and unmanned aerial vehicles to drone-capturing technology. FBI WARNS BATTLEFIELD-STYLE DRONE ATTACKS COULD REACH US: 'ONLY A MATTER OF TIME' Brigadier General Jason Rueschhoff, director of operations for U.S. Northern Command, told Fox News, "We are developing capability at a pace that is keeping ahead of our enemy, and that's really important. And that's what happens here." Fox News Digital reported at the start of the month that Joint Task Force – Southern Border was carrying out drone takedowns using specialized counter-drone equipment provided and integrated by other military units, according to a senior War Department official. The official said each operation was planned and closely coordinated with the Mexican military and border authorities to prevent interference or unintended conflicts between forces operating on either side of the border. articles.title: 3 takeaways from our new polling averages: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Scott Bland breaks down the numbers to know from our newly launched polling averages. Plus, Henry J. Gomez explains why Appalachia will be key to the outcome of Ohio’s Senate race. — Adam Wollner 3 takeaways from NBC News’ polling averages Analysis by Scott Bland NBC News launched new polling averages today, rounding up all the available public surveys on two critical measures of the political moment: President Donald Trump’s approval rating and which party voters say they’ll back for Congress this fall. Here’s what the new averages tell us: Democrats are at their strongest point yet this cycle. As Election Day draws nearer, the Democratic edge on the “generic ballot” — poll questions asking which party voters plan to support or want to see in control of Congress — is the widest it’s been (9 points) in Trump’s second term. The gap has expanded as we switched to calculating our polling average for likely voters instead of registered voters. Keep an eye out for undecided voters. That 9-point advantage for Democrats right now comes from a 52%-43% average. That leaves about 5% of respondents to all these polls unaccounted for, whether they’re undecided, not sure about voting, picking a third-party candidate or some other factor. There are ample reasons to think those remaining voters — and maybe some soft supporters on either side — could move one way or another in the next few weeks. Maybe the Democratic Party’s remaining unpopularity is too much for some voters to look past. Perhaps rising prices, the Iran war and other issues spark some 2024 Trump voters to back local Democratic candidates. Whatever ends up happening, that small slice will play a big role in 2026. So don’t forget about the undecided portion of a poll (or a polling average) when looking at the margin between Democrats and Republicans. What’s fueling Trump’s troubles? For all the importance of base turnout and polarization, independent voters make or break elections and presidencies. And independents are really, really sour on Trump right now. His approval rating with independents stands at 26% in the polling average, and they’re breaking toward Democrats on the generic ballot in a big way. Don’t ignore Trump’s numbers among Republicans, though. His approval rating has dipped about 10 points among the GOP since his second inauguration, and he’s facing some serious skepticism from parts of his party about the Iran war and the economy. Read more on our new polling averages → How race, religion and a private jet could make Appalachia a battleground in Ohio By Henry J. Gomez PORTSMOUTH, Ohio — Vivek Ramaswamy won Ohio’s Republican primary for governor in May with a landslide 82.4% of the vote. But Democrats see opportunity this fall in the wide swath of rural counties where Ramaswamy won by smaller margins against a largely unknown opponent. Ramaswamy underperformed his statewide vote share in 29 of the 32 counties classified as Appalachia. Seven of his 10 weakest counties are in the region that rings eastern and southern Ohio along the Ohio River. Amy Acton, Ramaswamy’s Democratic rival, has made repeated trips to the area, which gets less attention and has fewer voters than large metro areas such as Columbus and Cleveland. During a two-day swing last week, she visited Shawnee State University here across the river from Kentucky, and she stopped in Marietta, where she boasts an endorsement from the City Council president — a Republican. Acton is unlikely to win in places that have decisively backed President Donald Trump in recent elections. Her goal is to hold down Ramaswamy’s percentages there. “People are exhausted of being pitted against one another,” Acton, a physician and the state’s former health director, said after she toured an art gallery, a library and a 3D printing lab on Shawnee State’s campus. “They’re exhausted of the hate and chaos and vitriol, and they want us to just get back. They don’t really care what party you are.” The challenges Ramaswamy faces stem in part from a tough political climate for Republicans nationwide, according to conversations with more than a dozen Ohio activists and operatives from both parties. Trump, who backs Ramaswamy, faces low job approval ratings as he navigates an unpopular war with Iran and frustration over the cost of living. But there are challenges unique to Ramaswamy, a billionaire who struck it rich in biotech. He travels the state in a private plane at a time when affordability concerns — including a war-related rise in gas and diesel prices — are felt deeply in Appalachia. Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: Report shows Utah Valley University had several security issues on day of Charlie Kirk assassination
articles.summary: A report released Friday shows Utah Valley University (UVU) had several security issues on the day political commentator Charlie Kirk was assassinated on campus. The 158-page independent review for UVU stated that university staff and security personnel deferred critical decisionmaking to the Turning Point USA (TPUSA) team and failed to conduct a formal written security…
articles.body:
A report released Friday shows Utah Valley University (UVU) had several security issues on the day political commentator Charlie Kirk was assassinated on campus .

The 158-page independent review for UVU stated that university staff and security personnel deferred critical decisionmaking to the Turning Point USA (TPUSA) team and failed to conduct a formal written security assessment.

“Several key event-security decisions were deferred to TPUSA field representative even though UVU staff members raised concerns, including concerns related to holding the event in the outdoor Fountain Courtyard and use its own ticketing system rather than the University’s system,” the report read.

It continued that those decisions placed Kirk in an area that was “more difficult to control” and limited UVU’s ability to obtain information regarding crowd size and attendance.

In one instance, however, UVU Police Department Chief Jeffrey Long messaged Turning Point Security Supervisor Dan Flood, attempting to coordinate a meeting “to ensure that both groups had a shared understanding of the security posture,” but these face-to-face meetings never occurred.

This contrasts accusations made by lawyers for the Kirk family who sent a notice of claim to UVU, accusing the university of having no security plan and only six police officers working the event.

They also alleged a member of Turning Point USA texted Long before the event with security concerns about the specific rooftop where the shooter fired from.

Kirk was fatally shot while debating student Hunter Kozak, which marked one of the most prominent acts of political violence in 2025. Tyler Robinson was arrested and charged in connection with Kirk’s death for aggravated murder, along with six other counts. The murder case was sent to trial last month , where Robinson could face the death penalty if convicted.

During the shooting, the report also stated the university’s actions were “significantly inconsistent” with its policies.

The report concluded no personnel affiliated with UVU acted “in bad faith or in willful and wanton disregard for the safety of others.”

Brett Parkinson, an attorney for the Kirk family, told The Hill that the report “affirms the facts we laid out in our Notice of Claim: that UVU security was woefully understaffed and unprepared to manage the obvious risks associated with an event of this nature.”

“UVU hosted this event, and in doing so, assumed responsibility for the safety of all in attendance, including Charlie. The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement,” he continued. “Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU’s fatal shortcomings that day.”

Utah Valley University President Jon Anderson stated in a press release that the university’s “responsibility is to care for our community, learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations.”

He added that the report “provides additional recommendations” for UVU to guide its work in the future.

articles.title: Florida GOP nominee blasts 20-year Dem incumbent as a 'socialist' rubber-stamp with 'precious little to show'
articles.summary: Former Florida legislator Mike Beltran seeks to oust 10-term incumbent Kathy Castor in 14th district, arguing she has been ineffective and out of touch with constituents.
articles.body: Calling out federal waste and foreign aid subsidies while pointing to his own record of bucking party leadership in Tallahassee, GOP 14th congressional district nominee Mike Beltran promises to bring a sharp litigator’s cross-examination to Washington’s budget crisis. In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital detailing his bid to unseat 20-year Democratic incumbent Kathy Castor, the former Florida state representative laid out a case rooted in strict fiscal accountability, pledged to challenge even Republican leadership on bloated federal budgets, and warned of the Democrats' embrace of socialism. HOUSE CONSERVATIVES UNLEASH MULTIMILLION-DOLLAR MIDTERM BLITZ AGAINST DEM 'SOCIALIST' INSURGENCY Beltran argues that despite her lengthy tenure on Capitol Hill, the people of Tampa Bay have not been served well by Kathy Castor. "People in Tampa Bay have precious little to show for Kathy Castor's two decades of incumbency. She's had no major legislative initiatives. All she's really done is rename post offices. And all that's likely to happen if we reelect her is for her to rename every post office from Tampa to Timbuktu. "She votes with her party over 90% of the time, including radical socialists. She voted in lockstep with Nancy Pelosi and she's poised to elect the Speaker Hakeem Jeffries. And Speaker Hakeem Jeffries would appoint a Chair Raskin, a Chair Omar, a Chair Cortez, and those folks would push radical policies in Congress that are completely out of line with what Tampa families need." Beltran argues that in the Florida Legislature he served as an independent conservative voice, not automatically beholden to party leadership, and pledges to continue that approach in Washington. "I've had the courage to vote against special interests even when my own party had lost its way. I've voted against insurance companies, home builders, trial lawyers, I voted against various special interests…whenever somebody was doing something that wasn't good for Tampa families. "And I had that bipartisan record throughout my time, starting in 2019 and continuing through to 2024, unlike my opponent who discovered bipartisanship merely weeks ago. So I'm always going to do what's best for the communities that I represent, regardless of party, regardless of special interests, regardless of pressure. And that's what I'm proud of, having that independent voting record." Beltran argues that the United States needs to reexamine its military and geopolitical relationships, with an eye to fiscal prudence: "It cannot be a one-sided exchange. You cannot have a wealthy country like Germany spend under 2% of GDP on their military when we're spending over 5% of our GDP on our military budgets, about a trillion dollars. And a lot of that is spent overseas protecting other wealthy countries. "You see Ukraine and Israel, they're defending themselves from their adversaries. They're doing a good job of that. But we are borrowing $2 trillion a year from countries like China. And that's causing inflation. And what that says is that we don't have money to be sending, particularly to wealthy allies like Germany and Spain. "These are countries where we have bases, where we've had trouble getting basing privileges or overflight rights for the conflicts that we do need to engage in. And we shouldn't be subsidizing them anymore. "You see Israel spends over 10% of GDP on defense, as does South Korea. Those countries are carrying the weight of their own defense, but we don't see that from all of our NATO allies. And they're a lot closer to these rogue states, to these conflict regions than we are. They should be doing more, and they're doing less, and that's unacceptable." As an attorney, Beltran makes the case that he will bring a strong skill-set to Capitol Hill, to do away with business as usual and to fight for the citizens of Hillsborough County: "My legal skills are quite good. I'm a good cross examiner. I'll be good at scrutinizing witnesses who come before committees that I serve on. I've litigated in the federal courts, so I know the federal statutes. I know issues that need to be redressed. I know how to write statutes so that they can be easily applied by judges, so that attorneys can counsel their clients on what the law is and what they need to do to comply with that. "I'm proud to be a practicing attorney. I've helped a lot of businesses and individuals throughout Tampa Bay for almost 20 years. FIRST DATA CENTER BILL CLEARS HOUSE AS BOTH PARTIES SCRAMBLE FOR ANSWERS ON AFFORDABILITY "And my opponent is also an attorney, but she hasn't practiced in a very long time. She was, I think, a land use attorney, she says, before she was a county commissioner. But I don't think she brings that same skill-set. I've never seen her cross-examine a witness to any effect. And I haven't seen her apply her legal skills to any legislative initiative. In fact, it's kind of difficult to identify anything that she's enacted that's of any particular value to Tampa or otherwise." Kathy Castor has repeatedly voted against the interests of ordinary Americans in Florida's 14th district, Beltran argues: "Well, she opposed tax cuts for the middle class and working class and retirees. She opposed removing taxes on tips, removing taxes on Social Security, removing taxes on overtime. "And she wanted to pay, through taxpayer funds, for trans surgeries for children. And that was a very recent vote. That wasn't something that we have to reach into ancient history to find. And I opposed that. "I see no reason why a single mother here in Hillsborough County should be paying taxes to pay for trans surgeries for minors while she actually is being taxed on her overtime or her tips." Beltran pledges to confront the leadership of his own party if he disagrees with their policies, but also notes he will work with Democrats: "Obviously, we've had Republicans who have also spent too much money. And so I'm going to go to Washington. I'm going to work with my party, and I'll work across the aisle, and I'll work with any administration that's in power to identify waste, fraud, and abuse, identify unnecessary government programs, identify savings, and identify cost controls, and make sure that we are the fiscal conservatives that we say we are. "That's what's necessary to save this country because we need to balance the budget and we need pay down the debt and we need to live within our means, because if we don't balance our budget, then the budget will be balanced for us and it will be done when somebody cuts off our credit and people stop lending to us." Finally, as democratic socialist candidates have won Democratic primaries across the nation and in Florida, Beltran notes that Castor has consistently refused to condemn socialist ideology, or candidates with such views in her own party. "We see Kathy Castor, who's embraced Angie Nixon, who is one of those avowed socialist candidates. She said that her party was a big tent party, and that needs to be a very big tent to accommodate Angie Nixon…I'm not sure I'd like to be in a tent of any size with her, but my opponent welcomes her with open arms. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "And she's going to vote in lockstep with these socialists, first to elect Hakeem Jeffries and then to appoint these socialists to committee chairmanships. She's done very little to distance herself from the radicals within her party. Even as she masquerades recently as a moderate, she will empower the socialists. "And that's really what's at stake in November. It's not just me, it's not just Kathy Castor, it is the direction of the country and whether we're going to embrace these radical policies, or whether we are going to have economic growth and prosperity and safety here in the United States."

articles.body:
Appeals court sides with Pentagon on Anthropic blacklisting

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit sided with the Trump administration in its blacklisting of the artificial intelligence firm Anthropic , allowing the Pentagon to label the AI firm a supply chain risk.

The 2-1 ruling , issued Friday, rejected Anthropic’s challenge of the designation, finding the Department of Defense had “ample support” for its belief that the continued use of Anthropic’s Claude models by the agency or its contractors presented a national security risk.

The three-judge panel in D.C. specifically took up the question of whether the Pentagon and Secretary Pete Hegseth had the legal authority under a statute of the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act (FASCA) to declare Anthropic a supply chain risk.

“The Department reasonably feared that Anthropic might manipulate Claude’s design to prevent it from performing national-security functions that the Department deems contractually authorized and necessary,” Circuit Judge Gregory Kastas wrote for the majority.

Anthropic sued the Trump administration in March, challenging both the Pentagon’s designation — typically reserved for foreign adversaries — and President Trump’s directive for civilian agencies to stop using Anthropic’s products after negotiations fell apart over safety guardrails earlier this year.

Anthropic requested its technology not be used in fully autonomous lethal weapons or for the mass surveillance of Americans, while the Pentagon insisted it be allowed to use Anthropic’s Claude for “all lawful uses.”

“Because Anthropic was willing and able to enforce contractual restrictions through model training, the Department reasonably worried that ‘critical defense system’ supported by Claude might ‘fail to engage’ as the Department would expect,” Kastas wrote.

articles.title: Supreme Court blocks use of GOP-favored map in Missouri — again
articles.summary: The Supreme Court on Friday blocked a directive for Missouri Republicans to use their favored congressional map, again, making clear to officials they must return to an old design for November after the state’s messy redistricting battle. The decision is a blow for the GOP, which fought to use a more favorable 7-1 House map…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court on Friday blocked a directive for Missouri Republicans to use their favored congressional map , again, making clear to officials they must return to an old design for November after the state’s messy redistricting battle.

The decision is a blow for the GOP, which fought to use a more favorable 7-1 House map in time for the November midterms instead of the older 6-2 map.

Republicans had passed their 7-1 congressional lines last year and used it during their August primaries, but the high court’s decision means the Show Me State will now be using a different set of maps for the general election.

“In short, as a matter of state law, the 2022 map—not the 2025 map—must be used in the 2026 congressional election,” the court wrote in its unsigned opinion.

It’s the third time the battle reached the Supreme Court in as many weeks. In each round, the GOP has lost. The justices said ruling otherwise at this point would “usher in electoral chaos” since ballots are already being mailed.

The Show Me State has been roiled by several different lawsuits regarding Republicans’ new 7-1 House map, which was created amid pressure from President Trump and national Republicans as the GOP has sought to add pickup opportunities to the lower chamber ahead of the fall.

Republicans sought to dismantle Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s (D-Mo.) Kansas City-based district. But Cleaver appears poised to win reelection with the state reverting back to using its old lines.

The legal battle plunged into chaos earlier this month when Missouri’s top court ruled that a referendum over the congressional lines will now go before voters, meaning that the new 7-1 House map does not go into effect until it’s passed.

By that point, Missouri had already used the design to select primary winners. Several GOP congressional candidates began convincing a federal judge that reverting so late to the old map would be unconstitutional.

This Supreme Court previously lifted the judge’s order, appearing to signal that Republicans wouldn’t be able to redistrict in time for November. But that didn’t stop the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. On Monday, it issued a new ruling effectively reinstating the state’s 7-1 map. It was set to take effect next week.

That’s what led to the latest round at the Supreme Court. The referendum organizer fighting the GOP brought the new ruling back to the justices, seeking an emergency intervention.

“Given this Court’s two prior orders in this litigation, our conclusion that this was error should come as no surprise,” the court wrote Friday as it granted his request. The organizer emphasized that election officials had already started mailing out military and overseas ballots Saturday using the 6-2 House map. The Supreme Court’s decision allows election officials to proceed as usual, with no need to make last-minute changes to their ballots before the general election.

However, the late litigation is frustrating for candidates and voters. Election officials and contenders are racing to educate voters about who’s on their ballot and which congressional district they’re in with just weeks out from the election.

Politically, the Supreme Court’s decision has little impact on the national redistricting math as Republicans had only sought to add one pickup opportunity to their column in Missouri.

“At this late date, ordering reversion to the 2025 map in the midst of an ongoing election would usher in electoral chaos,” the court wrote in its opinion.

articles.title: Supreme Court for the third time rejects Republican redistricting push in Missouri
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — For the third time, the Supreme Court on Friday shut down efforts by Missouri Republicans to use a new congressional map in the midterm elections that are already underway.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — For the third time, the Supreme Court on Friday shut down efforts by Missouri Republicans to use a new congressional map in the midterm elections that are already underway. The court blocked an appeals court ruling that sought to revive the 2025 map despite two previous Supreme Court decisions and a ruling by the Missouri Supreme Court that ruled against Republicans on the same issue. There were no dissents. “At this late date, ordering reversion to the 2025 map in the midst of an ongoing election would usher in electoral chaos,” the ruling said. In doing so, the justices granted an emergency application filed by People Not Politicians, the group challenging the new map. “We are done with corrupt politicians trying to force their map into effect outside the process outlined in the Missouri constitution,” Richard von Glahn, executive director of People Not Politicians Missouri, said in a statement. “We have said from the beginning, people, not politicians will be the final deciders on this DC power grab.” The election will proceed using a 2022 map that includes six seats held by Republicans and two held by Democrats. The state has already started sending out ballots to military and overseas voters, and some absentee voting began Tuesday. The high court cited the fact that Missouri has already begun its voting processes in its argument. “This Court has repeatedly cautioned that ‘lower federal courts should not ‘alter the election rules’’ of a state ‘on the eve of an election,’” the ruling said. “The election is not merely upcoming; it has already started.” The proposed 2025 map would have eliminated one of the Democratic seats, held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver. The Missouri map was part of a nationwide push by Republicans at the urging of President Donald Trump to draw new congressional districts that would favor their candidates. Democrats in other states, including California, responded by drawing new maps, too. The St. Louis-based 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Monday ruled that the Republican-drawn Missouri map could be used, but it never went into effect. The Supreme Court’s ruling Tuesday overturns that decision. The appeals court had ruled the state had to use the 2025 map in part because the primary election had already taken place using it. But in a conflicting ruling, the Missouri Supreme Court said the 2022 map had to be used, while making it clear that Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, was to blame for the confusion. The state high court ultimately held Hoskins in contempt for his actions. In its ruling on Friday, the Supreme Court wrote that Hoskins “was well aware that conducting the August primary election with the 2025 map carried significant risks,” citing a May opinion from the state high court that made clear the new map would not go into effect ahead of the 2026 elections. The court battle started after opponents of the new map gained enough signatures to trigger a state referendum on whether it should be used. Under state law, whenever a state law is subject to a referendum, it is suspended until after the vote takes place. But Hoskins delayed a decision on whether the referendum push was legitimate until the eve of the primary. He rejected the proposal and ordered the new map to be used. The Missouri Supreme Court then quickly ruled that there were no grounds to reject the referendum proposal and that, with the issue being put to voters in November, the map should be put on hold and the 2022 districts used instead. The litigation seemed to be over until a new lawsuit was filed on Sept. 4 by Rick Brattin, the Republican nominee in the district held by Cleaver, as well as Rep. Bob Onder, R-Mo., and two voters. That moved the fight into federal court, where Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark ruled that the new map should be used. That decision ultimately led to the appeals court ruling and Supreme Court intervention.

articles.title: White House defends pro-Trump TV ads timed with midterms: ‘Patriotism isn’t partisan’
articles.summary: The White House defended the pro-President Trump television campaign that aired this week ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, saying that “patriotism isn’t partisan.” “The announcements are a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending — at home, at the border, and abroad,” the White House wrote in a…
articles.body:
The White House defended the pro-President Trump television campaign that aired this week ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, saying that “patriotism isn’t partisan.”

“The announcements are a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending — at home, at the border, and abroad,” the White House wrote in a press release . “These public service announcements are unapologetically American, clearly disclosed, and aimed at the country — not a line on the ballot.”

The 30-second commercial features Trump’s voice saying, “Together we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America” and “America will never be a communist country.” The song “Love Me” by JMSN, whose name is Christian Berishaj, plays in the background.

The ad used 2024 remarks from UFC President Dana White describing the president as “the toughest, most resilient person that I’ve ever met and nothing is going to stop him from fighting so hard for the country that he’s lost.”

The ad’s disclaimer reads, “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”

The White House cited multiple examples of presidents in the past using similar ad campaigns “to explain policy and make the case for the nation’s direction.”

The list included former President Biden’s “ We can do this ” vaccine commercials from 2021 that encouraged Americans to get vaccinated against COVID during the pandemic.

It also stated that “the announcements are very clearly not campaign ads; President Trump is not on the ballot and there is no call to action.”

Trump has endorsed a number of candidates in the upcoming midterm elections, and in August he encouraged voters to “pretend” he is “on the ballot.”

He invoked this same messaging tactic during a rally for Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) for her runoff election in the Palmetto State.

AdImpact, a political media monitoring company, estimated the Trump administration spent more than $400,000 to run the ads, according to The Associated Press . The outlet also reported that the ad is running on primetime and morning shows on CBS and various Fox News programming.

AdImpact wrote on social media that Trump’s July 4th advertisement began airing Friday. It featured Trump narrating alongside a montage of pictures of the president delivering remarks at Mount Rushmore.

Iran has shared a seven-day plan with the U.S. to end fighting between the two countries, reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart talks for a final peace deal, Tehran’s foreign minister told multiple outlets Thursday in New York City.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told a group of reporters at the UN General Assembly that “if certain conditions are met” by Washington, the strait would be opened at the end of the plan’s seven days.

Araghchi noted that the terms of the proposal, given to the U.S. through intermediators, closely matched commitments in the now dead 14-point Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) signed by Washington and Tehran in June. That deal unraveled amid renewed fighting in July.

articles.title: Francesca Hong says she regrets CNN interview about Thanksgiving
articles.summary: Francesca Hong, a former democratic socialist candidate in the Wisconsin gubernatorial race, said Friday she regrets her controversial CNN interview where she stated she wanted to “cancel Thanksgiving.” In an interview with WISN, a local ABC affiliate, anchor Matt Smith reflected on Hong’s time on the campaign trail and asked if there was anything she…
articles.body:
Francesca Hong, a former democratic socialist candidate in the Wisconsin gubernatorial race, said Friday she regrets her controversial CNN interview where she stated she wanted to “cancel Thanksgiving.”

In an interview with WISN , a local ABC affiliate, anchor Matt Smith reflected on Hong’s time on the campaign trail and asked if there was anything she would have done differently in the lead up to Wisconsin’s gubernatorial primaries in August.

“I was never going to cancel Thanksgiving. Actually, love to celebrate the holidays,” Hong said.

Ahead of the state’s Democratic primary, Hong’s past social media posts where she called for an end to Thanksgiving, where she stated that it “should have done this in 1621,” resurfaced. Backlash surrounding the democratic socialist grew when she defended her comments during a CNN interview in the week leading up to the primaries.

“I think there I wanted to make sure that people understood that there are multiple views, but views can evolve,” she said at the time.

Days later, in an interview with Politico, Hong walked back her take on Thanksgiving — telling the outlet she “actually loves” the holiday. Around the same time, she told The Hill that her original comments “could” have been made in jest.

When asked if she regretted the CNN interview and if she saw it as defining moment for her campaign in the lead up to the primaries, Hong responded, “It was a regrettable moment.”

“And I do regret that interview,” she concluded.

Hong added that she wished she would have leaned further into her Wisconsin roots during the campaign trail.

“I’m a daughter of Wisconsin, born and raised in this state. There’s nothing I love more than Packer games, Culvers and making sure that my community has the things that they need,” she said.

“We needed to reach more people with that message,” Hong added. “I’m incredibly proud of the movement that we built, the enthusiasm that is still there.”

Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley narrowly beat Hong in be the Democratic candidate in the race to replace retiring Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers (D). Despite polling from July placing Hong nearly 25 points ahead of Crowley, she lost to him by more than 3,000 votes when the race was called by Decision Desk HQ .

The loss marked a significant hit to the growing democratic socialist movement and gave moderate Democrats a much-needed boost ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
